questions.doc:
Taking Short Breaks at Work
Staff at one Calgary office have started a simple experiment: every hour, a soft chime reminds employees to stand up, stretch or walk for two minutes. The idea came from Helen Marsh, a team leader who noticed that her colleagues often complained of stiff backs by mid-afternoon. 'At first, people found the chime annoying,' she admits. 'Some even turned it off.' After a month, however, most of the team had changed their minds. Several said they felt more focused after a short walk, and fewer people took long coffee breaks. Marsh is careful not to make big claims. 'We're not scientists,' she says. 'But for a small change that costs nothing, the results have been encouraging.'
questions.q: How did employees react to the chime at first?
options: Most felt more focused right away.
Many found it irritating.
They asked for longer coffee breaks.
They complained of stiff backs.

explain.en: Marsh says: 'At first, people found the chime annoying. Some even turned it off.' Feeling more focused came later, after a month.
explain.fr: Marsh dit : « At first, people found the chime annoying. Some even turned it off. » Le sentiment d’être plus concentré n’est venu qu’après un mois.

Green Bin Program Expands to Apartment Buildings
Starting this fall, the City of Port Alder will offer green bins for food scraps to apartment and condo buildings with more than six units. Until now, only houses could take part. Building owners who want to join must apply online before August 31. Each participating building will receive large shared bins for the garbage room, plus one small kitchen container per unit. Residents can put fruit and vegetable peels, coffee grounds, bones and dirty paper towels in the bin, but not plastic bags, even those labelled 'compostable.' Collection will take place once a week. Buildings that do not apply this year can join next spring.
questions.q: Who must apply to join the program?
options: Owners of apartment buildings.
Each apartment's residents.
Buildings with fewer than six units.
Owners of single houses.

explain.en: The notice states: 'Building owners who want to join must apply online before August 31.' Residents simply use the bins once the building is in.
explain.fr: L’avis dit : « Building owners who want to join must apply online before August 31 ». Les résidents utilisent simplement les bacs une fois l’immeuble inscrit.

questions.doc:
Review: The Ferry Keeper
The Cove Street Players' new production tells the story of a ferry operator on a small island who refuses to retire. On paper, it doesn't sound like much. On stage, it is often moving. Gloria Mendes, in the title role, is excellent: funny, stubborn and, in the final scene, heartbreaking. The set is simple, just a dock, a bench and a lantern, but the lighting creates a convincing sense of fog and night. The second act is weaker; a subplot about a land developer feels rushed and is never really resolved. Still, this is community theatre at its best. Tickets are $18, and the show runs until November 9.
questions.q: What is the reviewer's overall opinion?
options: Mixed, mainly because of the set.
Positive, despite some weaknesses.
Very negative about the whole second act.
Negative, as the story is too simple.

explain.en: The reviewer praises the lead actor and lighting and calls it 'community theatre at its best', while noting that 'The second act is weaker'.
explain.fr: Le critique salue l’actrice principale et l’éclairage et parle de « community theatre at its best », tout en notant que « The second act is weaker ».

questions.doc:
Four Days, Same Work?
When Tallgrass Design, a 40-person graphic design firm in Saskatoon, announced it would test a four-day work week, some clients worried that projects would be delayed. Six months later, the company says the opposite has happened. Employees now work four nine-hour days, with Fridays off, and meetings are limited to 30 minutes. 'When you lose a day, you stop wasting time,' says founder Marc Leblanc. Not everyone is convinced. One designer, who asked not to be named, says the longer days are exhausting, especially for parents who must pick up children after school. Others report that client emails sent on Fridays simply pile up until Monday. Leblanc admits the model is not perfect, but says fewer employees have quit since the change, and he plans to continue the trial for another year.
questions.q: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Employees at a design firm are asking for a four-day week.
A firm has ended its four-day week experiment.
The new schedule mostly works, despite some drawbacks.
Clients have left a firm because of its new schedule.

explain.en: The company says projects were not delayed and fewer people quit, but the article also reports exhausting days and piled-up emails. The trial will continue another year.
explain.fr: L’entreprise dit que les projets n’ont pas pris de retard et que moins d’employés sont partis, mais l’article signale aussi des journées épuisantes et des courriels en attente.

questions.doc:
Opinion: Let Homeowners Build Laneway Suites
Our city faces a housing shortage, yet thousands of backyards sit empty. Allowing homeowners to build small laneway suites, separate cottages facing the back lane, would add homes without changing the character of our streets. Critics argue that these units will bring more cars and noise to quiet neighbourhoods. That concern is understandable, but it is exaggerated. A laneway suite is usually home to one or two people, often a family member or a young worker who cannot afford a full house. Others worry about parking. Here, the city could simply require that new suites be close to public transit. What we cannot afford is to keep saying no to every idea that changes our neighbourhoods even slightly. Doing nothing is also a choice, and it has a cost.
questions.q: What is the writer's main argument?
options: Homeowners should be paid to build laneway suites.
Laneway suites would add homes without hurting streets.
Laneway suites should be kept for family members.
The city should build more public transit in quiet areas.

explain.en: The writer says laneway suites 'would add homes without changing the character of our streets'. Transit is mentioned only as a way to deal with parking.
explain.fr: L’auteur affirme que ces logements « would add homes without changing the character of our streets ». Le transport en commun n’est cité que pour régler le stationnement.

questions.doc:
Letter: The Bike Lane Is Working, but Not for Everyone
I have cycled to work on Front Street for ten years, and the new protected bike lane has changed my daily trip. I no longer arrive at the office shaking after a close call with a delivery truck. So I was surprised to read last week's editorial calling the lane 'a costly mistake.' That said, the editorial raised one fair point. The new design makes it harder for people with disabilities to be dropped off at the medical clinic on the corner, since vehicles can no longer stop at the curb. This is a real problem, and it should be fixed with a proper loading zone, not used as an argument to remove the lane altogether.
Joanne Park, Kingsford
questions.q: Why did the writer send this letter?
options: To defend the bike lane while admitting one problem.
To complain about delivery trucks on Front Street.
To agree that the bike lane was a costly mistake.
To ask the clinic to move to another street.

explain.en: She disagrees with the editorial calling the lane 'a costly mistake' but admits it 'raised one fair point' about drop-offs at the clinic.
explain.fr: Elle conteste l’éditorial qui qualifie la piste de « costly mistake », mais reconnaît qu’il « raised one fair point » au sujet de l’accès à la clinique.

questions.doc:
Do Backyard Birds Prefer Messy Gardens?
For three summers, a team of volunteers in Pine Harbour, Nova Scotia, counted birds in 60 backyards. Half of the yards were neatly kept, with short lawns and few shrubs; the other half had been left partly wild, with tall grass, piles of branches and native plants. The results, published in the volunteers' own report, were striking: the 'messy' gardens attracted almost twice as many bird species on average. Project coordinator Ruth Abernathy is cautious about the conclusion, however. The wilder gardens, she notes, also tended to be larger and closer to the forest, which could explain part of the difference. 'We can't say tidiness alone is the cause,' she says. Still, she hopes the findings will encourage homeowners to leave at least one corner of their yard untouched. 'You don't have to give up your lawn,' she adds. 'Even a small pile of leaves in the fall can make a difference for insects, and therefore for the birds that eat them.'
questions.q: Why is Abernathy cautious about the results?
options: The neat yards attracted more of the rare bird species.
The study lasted only a single summer.
Other differences between yards may explain them.
The volunteers counted birds in different ways.

explain.en: She notes that the wilder gardens 'also tended to be larger and closer to the forest, which could explain part of the difference'. The study lasted three summers.
explain.fr: Elle souligne que les jardins sauvages « also tended to be larger and closer to the forest, which could explain part of the difference ». L’étude a duré trois étés.

questions.doc:
The Library Is Not Just About Books
Every few years, someone asks whether public libraries still matter when information is a click away. The question misunderstands what libraries do. Visit the Eastgate branch on a weekday afternoon and you will see students doing homework because their apartments are too crowded, seniors attending a smartphone workshop, a job seeker printing résumés, and a parent at story time with a toddler who has never owned a picture book. Very few of these people are there for 'information' in the narrow sense. They are there because the library is one of the last indoor places where you can stay for hours without being expected to buy anything. That is not a small thing. In a city where a coffee costs five dollars, a free, warm, quiet room is a public service as essential as a bus route. Cutting library hours to save money may look sensible in a spreadsheet. On the ground, it means closing the door on the people who have the fewest alternatives.
questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose?
options: To argue that libraries are an essential public space.
To propose new ways for libraries to save money.
To describe the programs offered at one library branch.
To explain how libraries are adapting to the internet.

explain.en: The writer says the library is 'one of the last indoor places where you can stay for hours' and calls it 'a public service as essential as a bus route'.
explain.fr: L’auteur dit que la bibliothèque est « one of the last indoor places where you can stay for hours » et la juge « as essential as a bus route ».

questions.doc:
From Classroom to Job Site
When Amira Saleh finished high school, her parents expected her to go to university. Instead, she enrolled in an electrical apprenticeship at Lakeshore Technical College, a program in which students spend about 80 percent of their time working for an employer and the rest in class. 'My friends thought I was giving up on my future,' she recalls. 'Now some of them are in debt and still looking for work, and I'm earning a salary while I learn.' Program director Tom Reilly says stories like Amira's are becoming more common, but he warns against presenting apprenticeships as an easy shortcut. The hours are long, the work is physically demanding, and students who fall behind in class can lose their placement. 'It's not the right choice for everyone,' he says. 'But it should be presented as a real choice, not as a backup plan for students who couldn't get into university.'
questions.q: What point does Reilly make?
options: Students should try university before an apprenticeship.
Apprenticeships are demanding but deserve equal respect.
Apprenticeships are an easy way to avoid student debt.
Apprenticeships are the best option for most students.

explain.en: Reilly warns they are not 'an easy shortcut' and 'not the right choice for everyone', but should be 'a real choice, not a backup plan'.
explain.fr: Reilly prévient que ce n’est pas « an easy shortcut » ni « the right choice for everyone », mais que cela doit être « a real choice, not a backup plan ».

questions.doc:
The Tyranny of the Headline
Most of us now meet the news not in articles but in headlines, scrolled past on a phone, glimpsed between messages, shared by a friend who may not have read further either. This would matter less if headlines were neutral summaries. They are not, and they were never meant to be. A headline's job is to make you stop. The more crowded the feed, the harder it must work, and the easier it is for 'Council considers options for park' to become 'Park could vanish, residents fear.' Neither version is false. One is simply more likely to be clicked. Editors I have spoken to are not cynical about this; most are uneasy. They point out, fairly, that a perfectly accurate headline nobody reads informs no one. The trouble is that readers increasingly treat the headline as the story itself, forming opinions on a dozen words written to provoke. The solution is not to blame journalists, nor to demand that readers click every link. It may be more modest: a habit of asking, before reacting, what the headline is designed to make me feel, and whether the article, if I read it, would make me feel the same.
questions.q: What is the author's attitude toward editors?
options: Understanding of the pressure they face.
Indifferent to their point of view.
Critical of their dishonest headlines.
Admiring of their neutral summaries.

explain.en: The author says editors 'are not cynical' but 'uneasy', and that they point out, 'fairly', that an unread headline informs no one. The tone is sympathetic.
explain.fr: L’auteur dit que les éditeurs « are not cynical » mais « uneasy », et qu’ils font remarquer, « fairly », qu’un titre non lu n’informe personne. Le ton est compréhensif.

questions.doc:
In Defence of the Imperfect Lawn
Every spring, a quiet competition begins on suburban streets. The prize is a lawn of uniform green, free of dandelions, clover and any other sign that nature has opinions of its own. We rarely ask why we want this. The perfect lawn is a demanding ideal: it requires regular watering, frequent mowing and, often, products whose main purpose is to kill everything except one kind of grass. I do not wish to lecture anyone. I mowed my own lawn every Saturday for years, and I understood the pleasure of a neat edge. But when a dry summer and a broken mower forced me to let things go, something unexpected happened. Clover filled the bare patches, bees appeared, and my lawn stayed greener during the drought than my neighbours' did. My neighbours were polite about it. One of them asked, with real concern, whether I was 'going through something.' Perhaps I was. What I discovered is that the tidy lawn is less a natural preference than a social signal, proof that we are keeping up. The question is whether that signal is still worth what it costs.
questions.q: What does the neighbour's question suggest?
options: The neighbour was worried about the long drought.
An untidy lawn may be seen as a sign of personal trouble.
The writer had been rude to several people living on the street.
The neighbour wanted advice about growing clover.

explain.en: Asking 'with real concern' whether the writer was 'going through something' shows that a neglected lawn is seen as a sign of personal difficulty.
explain.fr: Demander « with real concern » si l’auteur était « going through something » montre qu’une pelouse négligée est perçue comme le signe de difficultés personnelles.

questions.doc:
Why I Reread
Friends sometimes look at me with pity when they see me reading a novel I have read three times before. With so many new books published every year, they ask, isn't rereading a waste of time? I understand the logic, but I think it rests on a misunderstanding of what a book is for. A first reading is driven by curiosity: we want to know what happens. That hunger is powerful, but it is also a little greedy; we rush past sentences to reach the next turn of the plot. On a second reading, the suspense is gone, and something else takes its place. We notice how the author prepared the ending in the first chapter, how a minor character was quietly important all along. By the third reading, the book has not changed, but I have, and so it reads differently. A novel I found romantic at twenty seems sad at forty. In this sense, rereading is not the opposite of discovery. It is discovery of a different kind, less about the book, perhaps, and more about the reader. None of this is an argument against new books. It is only a defence of the old ones, which are too often treated like meals: finished once, and never ordered again.
questions.q: According to the writer, what changes from one reading to the next?
options: The book, which reveals new events.
The suspense, which grows each time.
The plot, which the reader slowly forgets over time.
The reader, who brings a new perspective.

explain.en: The writer says 'the book has not changed, but I have, and so it reads differently', giving the example of a novel romantic at twenty and sad at forty.
explain.fr: L’auteur écrit « the book has not changed, but I have, and so it reads differently », avec l’exemple d’un roman romantique à vingt ans et triste à quarante.
